name: Data Structures & Algorithms
subject: dsa
description: Arrays, linked lists, trees, graphs, sorting and searching

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in an array by index?
questions.explanation: Array access by index is O(1) — constant time — because the memory address is calculated directly.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm has the best average-case time complexity?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort has O(n log n) average and worst-case complexity, making it one of the most efficient general-purpose sorting algorithms.

questions.question: In a singly linked list, which operation is O(1)?
questions.explanation: Inserting at the head of a singly linked list is O(1) — just update the head pointer. All other options require traversal.

questions.question: Which data structure is best for implementing a breadth-first search (BFS)?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a Queue (FIFO) to explore nodes level by level. DFS uses a Stack (or recursion).

questions.question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST) property?
options: Parent is always the largest node
questions.explanation: In a BST: left subtree values < node value < right subtree values. This property enables O(log n) search.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Merge Sort?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort requires O(n) extra space for the auxiliary arrays used during the merge step.

questions.question: What does a Hash Map use to store values?
options: Sequential array slots via a hash function
questions.explanation: A hash map uses a hash function to compute an index into an array where the value is stored, giving O(1) average access.

questions.question: What is the height of a balanced binary tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: A balanced binary tree has height O(log n). This is why balanced BSTs give O(log n) search/insert/delete.

questions.question: Which traversal visits nodes in Left-Root-Right order?
questions.explanation: In-order traversal: Left → Root → Right. For a BST, this visits nodes in sorted (ascending) order.

questions.question: What is a Min-Heap property?
options: Parent is always greater than children
Parent is always smaller than or equal to children
All leaves are at the same level
The root holds the maximum value
questions.explanation: In a Min-Heap, every parent node is smaller than or equal to its children. The minimum element is always at the root.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
questions.explanation: Quick Sort's worst case is O(n²), which occurs when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g., sorted input with bad pivot).

questions.question: What is a graph with no cycles called?
questions.explanation: A graph with no cycles is called an acyclic graph. A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is used in task scheduling.

questions.question: Two-pointer technique is most efficient for which problem on a sorted array?
options: Finding a pair that sums to a target
questions.explanation: Two pointers (one from each end) efficiently finds pairs summing to a target in O(n) time on a sorted array.

questions.question: What does Dynamic Programming optimize by storing?
options: Time by caching results of subproblems (memoization)
questions.explanation: DP avoids redundant computation by storing (memoizing) results of overlapping subproblems.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting into a sorted linked list at the correct position?
questions.explanation: You must traverse the list to find the correct position — up to n nodes — giving O(n) time.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm cannot work correctly when:
options: The graph has negative edge weights
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy approach breaks with negative edge weights. Use Bellman-Ford for graphs with negative edges.

questions.question: What is a deque?
options: A tree with two children per node
A double-ended queue allowing insert/delete at both ends
A queue where priority determines order
A special type of hash map
questions.explanation: A deque (double-ended queue) supports O(1) insertion and deletion at both the front and back.

questions.question: In Big O notation, what does O(1) mean?
options: The algorithm runs in exactly 1 second
The algorithm's runtime is constant regardless of input size
The algorithm uses 1 unit of memory
questions.explanation: O(1) = constant time complexity. The operation takes the same time regardless of how large the input is.

questions.question: What problem does a Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) data structure efficiently solve?
options: Detecting if two elements are in the same connected component
questions.explanation: Union-Find supports near-O(1) union and find operations, efficiently detecting connected components and cycles.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a stack implemented via array vs linked list?
options: Array stack is O(log n); linked list is O(1)
Array stack has fixed capacity; linked list stack is dynamically sized
Array stack uses FIFO; linked list stack uses LIFO
Linked list cannot implement a stack
questions.explanation: Array-based stacks have a fixed maximum capacity (or need resizing). Linked-list stacks grow dynamically without a preset limit.
